title: 1 Kings 13:11–19
context: An old prophet living in Bethel hears what the man of God did and rides after him. Finding him resting under an oak, he invites him home. When the man of God repeats the LORD's command, the old prophet claims that an angel told him to bring him back. The narrator says plainly, "He lied to him," and the man of God goes back and eats.

verses.text: Now an old prophet lived in Bethel, and one of his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told their father the words which he had spoken to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: An old prophet in Bethel hears from his sons what the man of God did and said. Arminian readers note that this prophet lives at the center of Jeroboam's false worship yet apparently said nothing against it himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator introduces this prophet without explaining his motives. His presence in Bethel, silent while Jeroboam's altar stood, raises questions the story leaves partly open.

verses.text: Their father said to them, “Which way did he go?” Now his sons had seen which way the man of God went, who came from Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The old prophet asks which way the man of God went. Arminian readers note that he takes deliberate steps to find him, suggesting a planned intention, though the text does not state his reasons.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that interpreters suggest different motives, such as curiosity, a desire for fellowship, or a wish to test or undermine the man of God. The text does not settle the question.

verses.text: He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” So they saddled the donkey for him; and he rode on it.
verses.arminianNotes: He has his donkey saddled and rides after the man of God. Arminian readers see the pursuit as a real choice with real consequences, both for the old prophet and for the one he seeks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how quickly the old prophet acts. The narrative builds suspense as the man of God's faithfulness is about to be tested by someone who claims to share his calling.

verses.text: He went after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak. He said to him, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” He said, “I am.”
verses.arminianNotes: He finds the man of God resting "under an oak." Arminian readers note that the man of God has paused on his journey, perhaps weary, which may have made him more vulnerable to the coming temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the detail without pressing it too far. Some see the stop as a lapse in urgency, while others see only a natural rest; either way, the test that follows is the main point.

verses.text: Then he said to him, “Come home with me and eat bread.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Come home with me and eat bread." Arminian readers note that the invitation repeats the king's offer from verse 7, now coming from a fellow prophet, which makes the temptation harder to recognize.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with the king's invitation. The same temptation returns in a more persuasive form, showing how testing often comes from unexpected and seemingly trustworthy sources.

verses.text: He said, “I may not return with you, nor go in with you. I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: The man of God refuses again, repeating his commitment. Arminian readers see that he still knows and states God's command clearly, so his later disobedience will not be due to ignorance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man of God's refusal shows he understood his orders. The test now turns on whether he will hold to the word God gave him personally against a contrary claim.

verses.text: For it was said to me by the LORD’s word, ‘You shall eat no bread or drink water there, and don’t turn again to go by the way that you came.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "For it was said to me by the LORD's word." Arminian readers note that the man of God grounds his refusal in God's direct command, the right foundation for resisting temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man of God appeals to the word he received directly from God. Scripture consistently teaches that God's clear word must govern even when others claim new revelation.

verses.text: He said to him, “I also am a prophet as you are; and an angel spoke to me by the LORD’s word, saying, ‘Bring him back with you into your house, that he may eat bread and drink water.’ ” He lied to him.
verses.arminianNotes: The old prophet claims an angel spoke to him, and the narrator adds, "He lied to him." Arminian readers see deception wrapped in religious authority, and a man of God who chooses to accept it without testing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Deuteronomy 13:3, where God may allow a false word "testing you." Paul later warns against even "an angel from heaven" bringing a contrary message (Galatians 1:8). God's direct word stands above such claims.

verses.text: So he went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water.
verses.arminianNotes: The man of God goes back, eats, and drinks. Arminian readers see a real failure of obedience: he had a clear command and chose to set it aside on another's word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet who resisted a king falls to a fellow prophet. Both traditions see a sober lesson that faithfulness must be tested against God's word, not against claims to authority.
